::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py pca`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**How do we reveal independent directions inside a matrix?**

Decompositions turn a difficult transformation into simpler factors. Eigenvectors reveal invariant directions when available; SVD works for arbitrary rectangular matrices; Cholesky applies to symmetric positive-definite systems. Rank approximation formalises which information is retained.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
A=U\Sigma V^\top,\qquad A_k=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sigma_j u_j v_j^\top
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

For A=diag(3,1), keeping the largest singular component retains diag(3,0) and incurs squared Frobenius reconstruction error 1. We trade one direction of information for a simpler representation.

## What to pay attention to

An invertible matrix need not be diagonalizable; a matrix may be symmetric without being positive definite. Match the factorisation to the hypotheses.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
